newsitem.title: USA: Simpson tells of contemplating suicide.
newsitem.headline: Simpson tells of contemplating suicide.

text.p: O.J. Simpson lost his composure on the witness stand on Monday as he related to jurors in his civil trial how police told him his two children did not see the mutilated bodies of their mother and a friend.

Simpson also said he contemplated suicide during the famous slow-speed freeway chase on the day he was due to surrender to police and was charged with the June 12, 1994, murders of ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman.
"I was feeling a lot of pain ... I just wanted to go to Nicole's grave. I was feeling, I guess, suicidal. I just wanted my pain to end," the former football star said.

Simpson, who was acquitted of the murders by a criminal court jury in October 1995 and is now battling a wrongful death lawsuit brought by the families of the victims, choked up at one point during Monday's testimony when he described asking police in a telephone call from his Chicago hotel room if his young children, Sydney and Justin, were safe.

"The first thing I was told was that my kids were alright but they were in a police station, and that concerned me. I wanted to know if my kids had been exposed to anything and he (Det. Ron Phillips) said 'No,' that they had been taken out the back (of Nicole Brown Simpson's condominium) and they didn't see anything," Simpson said in a breaking voice.
The two victims were stabbed and slashed to death on the front walkway of the condominium.

Simpson, losing his composure for the first time in nearly four days on the witness stand, was given a glass of water and breathed deeply before continuing. He said Phillips had told him his ex-wife had been murdered and he learned there was a second victim from his eldest daughter from a previous marriage, Arnelle.
He was also told by police they were not releasing any information to the media, which was why he did not tell anyone in Chicago what had happened, he said.

Talking about visiting his ex-wife's grave on June 17, when he was supposed to surrender, he said he was driven to the cemetery south of Los Angeles by his close friend, Al "A.C." Cowlings, but they were unable to get to the gravesite because a police car was parked at the entrance gate.
He said the two sat in a nearby orange grove for a while and when Cowlings went to a restroom Simpson got in the back seat of the car and took out a gun.

"I was in a lot of pain. I was missing Nicole. My kids didn't cry. I guess they had attacked me somewhat and that hurt me and I guess I just didn't know what to do," he said. It was not clear to whom he was referring when he said "they."

Asked why he did not go through with killing himself, he replied, "A.C., and my mom told me years ago that you can't go to heaven if you commit suicide and I was dealing with that, and thank God for A.C."

Simpson said he was asked by Juditha Brown, Nicole Brown Simpson's mother, shortly after the murders if he had anything to do with the killings. "She really got right up in my face and asked me. I told her, 'No I didn't, Judy, I love Nicole.'"
Asked by defence attorney Robert Baker if he ever thought that he was responible for his ex-wife's death, Simpson replied, "Not at any time, and I wouldn't, because I wasn't."

Asked why he volunteered to take a blood test at police headquarters shortly after returning to Los Angeles from Chicago on the day after the murders, Simpson said, "Because I didn't do anything and I was innocent. If it would help them (police) I'd do whatever I could to help them."
After his friendly examination by Baker, Simpson was confronted by a much more hostile Daniel Petrocelli, lead attorney for the plaintiffs, who accused him of lying.
"You have lied repeatedly to this jury, haven't you?" asked Petrocelli. "No," Simpson countered.
"You have lied repeatedly throughout your life, haven't you?" Petrocelli persisted. "No," Simpson replied.

Asked if he had lied to his first wife, Marquerite, when he started dating Nicole Brown Simpson while he was still married, Simpson said: "Morally it was dishonest of me, but I don't look on it as a lie."
